newsitem.title: USA: Downsizing reduces corporate blood donations.
newsitem.headline: Downsizing reduces corporate blood donations.

text.p: As big employers downsize and redistribute their personnel over more locations, it is becoming harder to collect blood from their plants and offices, American Red Cross officials say.

Since business traditionally accounts for about one-quarter of the six million pints of blood the Red Cross collects each year, the shortfall is contributing to spot shortages of blood around the country and has hiked the Red Cross' collection costs.
"It takes more effort to get the same number of donations from business today as in the past," said Brian McDonough, chief operating officer of American Red CrossBiomedical Services, Washington, D.C.

"More and more companies are distributing employees to multiple sites," McDonough said. "A company that had 600 or 700 employees in one location now might have three or four locations, and people who work at home who used to work at a company are no longer accessible to us as they were in the past."
Despite stepped up efforts, McDonough described ARC's blood collections in recent years as "flat."

"Where employers are trying to get more productivity out of workers, they're unable to share those (human) resources as well as before," said John Forbes, chief executive officer of the Red Cross' Missouri-Illinois region, based in St. Louis.

"More organizations have downsized, putting more responsibility on people and leaving them less time for doing charitable types of things," Forbes explained. "Our blood drives in recent years have become smaller. There are times during the year when the blood supply is in critical shape."
"Corporate blood drives that might have averaged 70 units (pints) of blood 10 years ago today are averaging 45 to 50 units," Forbes said.
According to Eddy Leon, the Red Cross' Blood Services manager for Dade County, Fla., "We always run short in the winter because there are more accidents and operations during the holidays."

"Employers have to do more to motivate and educate employees and make it convenient for the bloodmobile at their workplace," Leon said. His goal is to get one in five employees at a company to donate.

Motivating employees "takes a lot of upfront communication," said Lolly Walton, benefits coordinator at Ryder System Inc. in Miami. Ryder has 10 "blood captains" circulating during its four annual blood drives to sign up donors among its 1,100 headquarters employees.

Donors get a free lunch and are pampered with snacks and a movie in the corporate recreation room, raffle tickets for Miami Marlins baseball games, and $25 supermarket gift certificates. The effort has netted about 500 pints of blood a year for the Red Cross.

"It would be very very helpful to us to have more employers set aside time (for blood drives)," said Forbes. Accordingly, he has launched a regional mailing campaign and is "cold-calling" at smaller firms.

"We aim to take our collection activity to the smaller businesses and we're putting together a mini-mobile program to take a smaller staff to the smaller corporate setting, where we collect a dozen units of blood," Forbes said.
"What we're trying to do," McDonough of the Red Cross said, "is to learn how to go after smaller groups more efficiently. We don't have the ability to collect more blood from the groups that exist."
Employers who want the Red Cross to arrange a blood drive on their premises or to have their employees shuttled to the nearest blood collection site can call 1-800-GIVE-LIFE, McDonough said.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a freelance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
